paper.title: Deep Learning for ECG Analysis: Benchmarks and Insights from PTB-XL

project.title: Can a Small Model Tell a Normal Heartbeat from an Abnormal One?
project.question: Using the public PTB-XL ECG dataset, how well does a small convolutional network separate normal from abnormal ECGs compared with a simple feature-based baseline, and which abnormal classes are hardest?
project.hypothesis: A small 1D CNN trained on the 100 Hz recordings will score higher ROC-AUC than logistic regression on hand-made features, and errors will concentrate in classes with subtle waveform changes.
data: PTB-XL v1.0.3 from PhysioNet (CC BY 4.0), 100 Hz records
risks: Downloading the full dataset is slow on some connections; start with the 100 Hz records only.
Training a CNN on a CPU can be slow; use a free Colab runtime or fewer leads.
This is a learning project, not a medical device: results must not be used to diagnose anyone.

milestones.title: Explore the ECG data
milestones.deliverable: Notebook with ECG plots for each diagnostic superclass and a table of label counts

stuck.label: I can't load the ECG signal files
hints: Look at the files next to each record. Which ones describe the signal, and which ones hold the numbers?
PhysioNet stores signals in the WFDB format: a header file describes the leads and sampling rate, and a data file holds the samples. The wfdb Python package can read both together.

A skeleton you can fill in:
```python
import wfdb
record = wfdb.rdsamp(___)  # path to one record, without the file extension
signal, info = record
print(signal.shape, info[___])
```

stuck.label: I don't understand what the labels mean
hints: Open the metadata table and find the column that lists the codes for each ECG. Where does the dataset explain those codes?
Each ECG has one or more SCP-ECG statement codes. A second table maps every code to a diagnostic superclass such as normal, myocardial infarction or conduction disturbance.
Analogous example: if a shop table lists product codes, a second table maps each code to a department. Join them to count items per department, then do the same with ECG codes and superclasses.

stuck.label: My plots look like noise
hints: How many seconds of signal are you plotting, and is it one lead or all twelve on top of each other?
Each record has 12 leads sampled over 10 seconds. Plot one lead against time in seconds (sample index divided by the sampling rate) so the repeating heartbeats become visible.

Skeleton:
```python
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
t = np.arange(signal.shape[0]) / ___  # sampling rate
plt.plot(t, signal[:, ___])  # choose one lead
plt.xlabel("seconds"); plt.show()
```

milestones.title: Build labels and splits
milestones.deliverable: Script that makes a normal/abnormal label and uses the recommended folds, plus a class-balance table

stuck.label: Some ECGs have more than one label
hints: For your question, what does it mean for an ECG to be normal? What should happen if a record has a normal code and another code?
PTB-XL is multi-label: one ECG can belong to several superclasses. For a binary task you need a clear rule, written down before you look at model results.

Analogous example: a fruit tagged both 'ripe' and 'bruised' should probably not count as 'perfect'. Write a similar rule for 'normal only' versus 'anything abnormal', then test it on a few records by hand.

stuck.label: I don't know how to split the data
hints: Read the dataset page again. Does it already suggest which part to train on and which part to test on?

The recommended split uses the stratified fold column: one range of folds for training, one fold for validation and one for testing. Folds keep all ECGs of the same patient together, which prevents leakage.

Skeleton:
```python
train = meta[meta.strat_fold <= ___]
val = meta[meta.strat_fold == ___]
test = meta[meta.strat_fold == ___]
```

stuck.label: My classes are unbalanced
hints: How many normal and how many abnormal records are in your training folds? Write both numbers in your notebook.
Class imbalance changes how you should read accuracy. ROC-AUC looks at the ranking of scores across all thresholds, so it is less affected by the balance than accuracy is.
Analogous example: if 9 of 10 emails are not spam, a filter that marks nothing as spam is right most of the time but useless. Compare that idea with your own class counts.

milestones.title: Feature-based baseline
milestones.deliverable: Logistic regression on simple features with a validation ROC curve and AUC

stuck.label: I don't know which features to use
hints: Look at your plots from milestone 1. What differs between a normal ECG and an abnormal one that you could measure with a number?
Simple signal features include heart rate from the time between R-peaks, the spread of the signal, and the width of the main spike. Each ECG becomes one row of numbers.

Skeleton:
```python
def features(sig, fs):
    hr = ___  # heart rate from R-peak spacing
    spread = ___  # e.g. standard deviation of one lead
    return [hr, spread]
```

stuck.label: I'm not sure how to compute ROC-AUC
hints: What does your model output for each ECG: a hard label, or a probability-like score?
ROC-AUC needs scores, not hard labels. scikit-learn has a function that takes the true labels and the scores and returns the area under the ROC curve.
Analogous example: rank ten students by a practice-test score and check how often a student who passed the real test is ranked above one who failed. ROC-AUC measures that kind of ranking quality.

stuck.label: My baseline score seems too good
hints: Which data did the model see during training, and which data did you score it on?
A score that looks too good often means data leakage: information from the evaluation set got into training, for example through scaling fitted on all data or through the same patient in two folds.
Checklist skeleton: fit the scaler on ___ only; transform train, validation and test with that same scaler; confirm no patient id appears in both ___ and ___.

milestones.title: Small CNN
milestones.deliverable: 1D CNN trained on the signals and a table comparing it with the baseline on the test fold (evaluated once)

stuck.label: My CNN does not learn at all
hints: Plot the training loss for each epoch. Does it go down at all, stay flat, or jump around?
A flat loss often comes from inputs on very different scales, a learning rate that is too high or too low, or labels that do not match the inputs. Normalizing each lead helps neural networks train.

Skeleton of a tiny 1D CNN:
```python
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv1d(___, 16, kernel_size=7), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(16, ___))
```

stuck.label: Training is too slow on my laptop
hints: Which part takes the time: loading the files, or the training loop itself?
You can cut training cost by using the 100 Hz records, fewer leads, a smaller network, or caching the loaded signals in one array file instead of reading thousands of small files every epoch.
Analogous example: copying 1,000 photos one by one is slower than copying one zip file. Save your signals once with numpy and reload that single file in later sessions.

stuck.label: I don't know if the CNN is really better
hints: Did you evaluate both models on exactly the same ECGs, and how many times did you look at the test fold?

A fair comparison uses the same split and the same metric, tunes choices on the validation fold only, and evaluates on the test fold once at the end. Repeating runs with different random seeds shows how much scores vary.
Table skeleton for your report: model | validation AUC | test AUC | runs (seeds) | notes. Fill one row for the baseline and one for the CNN.

milestones.title: Error analysis and report
milestones.deliverable: 4-page report: method, results, which abnormal classes the models miss most, limitations

stuck.label: I don't know how to find which classes are hard
hints: Among the abnormal ECGs your model scored as normal, which superclasses appear most often?
Error analysis groups mistakes by a property you already have, here the original superclass. Comparing error rates across groups shows where the model struggles.

Skeleton:
```python
missed = test[(test.y == 1) & (test.score < ___)]
print(missed[___].value_counts())  # superclass column
```

stuck.label: I'm not sure what to put in my report
hints: Could a classmate repeat your work from your report alone? What would they still need to ask you?
A short research report usually has a question, data and method, results with one main table or figure, a discussion of errors, and limitations. The paper you started from follows a similar order.
Outline skeleton: 1. Question and why it matters, 2. Data (PTB-XL, folds), 3. Methods (baseline, CNN), 4. Results table, 5. Hard classes, 6. Limitations, including that this is not a medical tool.

stuck.label: I'm worried my results are wrong
hints: Which single step of your pipeline would you check first if someone said your numbers were too high?

Common checks are re-running from a clean notebook, confirming the split rule, and comparing your baseline with the scale of results reported in the paper's repository. Differences are fine if you can explain them.
Analogous example: a recipe that turns out differently in two kitchens is checked step by step, starting with the ingredients. Do the same with your data, split, model and metric, in that order.

quiz.question: You load the PTB-XL metadata with pandas. Which call shows the first five rows?
quiz.explanation: DataFrame.head() returns the first rows, five by default.

quiz.question: Which expression keeps only the rows whose fold number is at most 8?
quiz.explanation: Boolean indexing with a condition inside df[...] keeps the matching rows.

quiz.question: A 10-second ECG lead recorded at 100 Hz contains how many samples?
quiz.explanation: 100 samples per second times 10 seconds gives 1,000 samples.

quiz.question: Why might you prefer the 100 Hz version of PTB-XL for a laptop project?
options: Fewer samples per record means less memory and faster training
quiz.explanation: The same recordings at a lower sampling rate are five times smaller than the 500 Hz version.

quiz.question: What does ROC-AUC measure?
options: How many features the model uses
The percentage of correct labels at one threshold
How well the model's scores rank positive cases above negative ones across all thresholds
quiz.explanation: AUC summarizes the ROC curve, which is built from every possible threshold.

quiz.question: A model that assigns random scores would have an ROC-AUC close to which value?
quiz.explanation: Random scores rank a positive above a negative about half the time.

quiz.question: Why does PTB-XL put all ECGs from one patient in the same fold?
options: To make the folds equal in size
So the model is not tested on a patient it already saw in training
quiz.explanation: The same patient in train and test would leak information and inflate the score.

quiz.question: When should you use the test fold?
options: Once, at the end, after all choices were made on the validation fold
quiz.explanation: Repeatedly tuning on the test set turns it into a second validation set and overstates performance.

guides.why: Load the metadata table and the signal files.
guides.summary: pandas stores tables as DataFrames. You can read a CSV file, look at a few rows, select columns and keep only the rows that meet a condition. For PTB-XL, the metadata table lists one ECG per row with its labels and fold number.
steps: Read a CSV file into a DataFrame
Select columns and filter rows with a condition
guides.practice: Load any small CSV file and count how many rows have each value in one column.

guides.why: An ECG is a time series; 100 Hz means 100 samples per second per lead.
guides.summary: A signal is a value measured over time. The sampling rate says how many measurements are taken each second. An ECG lead at 100 Hz has 100 values for every second, and plotting them against time shows the heartbeat shape.
steps: Learn what a time series is
Understand sampling rate and its unit (Hz)
Plot one lead and identify heartbeats
guides.practice: Make a sine wave with numpy at two sampling rates and plot both to see the difference.

guides.why: The paper compares models with ROC-AUC, so you will too.
guides.summary: Binary classification sorts items into two groups. Many models output a score, and a threshold turns it into a label. The ROC curve shows the trade-off between catching positives and raising false alarms at every threshold, and the area under it summarizes ranking quality.
steps: See how a threshold turns scores into labels
Draw an ROC curve from scores
Compute the area under the curve with scikit-learn
guides.practice: Invent ten scores and labels by hand, sort them, and sketch the ROC curve on paper.

guides.why: PTB-XL keeps each patient in one fold; mixing them would inflate your score.
guides.summary: Models are trained on one part of the data, tuned on another and tested on a third. Leakage happens when information from the evaluation data reaches training, making results look better than they are. Keeping each patient in a single fold is one way PTB-XL prevents it.
steps: Learn why three splits are used
Find the fold column and the recommended split
List common leakage sources such as scaling on all data
Check that no patient appears in two splits
guides.practice: Write down three ways leakage could happen in an ECG project and how you would check each one.
